justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere around 490–495 for the underlying asset (which appears to be SPY or a similar broad equity index given the price range). For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price with only slight upward bias, reflecting the general long-run positive drift of equities and an assumption of no imminent major catalyst. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, and the one-month estimate continued that gentle upward trajectory, consistent with historical annualized returns of roughly 8–10% for U.S. large-cap equities translated into shorter time horizons.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using typical realized volatility for this asset class. At one day, the narrow band of roughly plus or minus 1.7% reflects the fact that daily moves in broad equity indices are usually contained, with standard deviations historically around 1% per day. At one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 7%, and at one month it expands further to about plus or minus 15% around the point estimate. These widths are broadly consistent with annualized volatility in the 15–20% range, scaled down to the appropriate time horizon using a square-root-of-time approximation. I also gave the distributions a slight positive skew to reflect the asymmetric upside potential over longer horizons.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden macroeconomic shock such as a surprise Federal Reserve policy decision, an unexpected inflation print, or a significant geopolitical escalation. On the downside, a rapid deterioration in credit markets, a banking sector stress event, or a sharp earnings disappointment from major index constituents could easily breach the lower bounds. Conversely, a dovish pivot by central banks, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could drive prices above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where compounding uncertainty makes tail outcomes more plausible.

It is also worth noting that my confidence intervals, while constructed to be 90% coverage intervals, are inherently model-dependent and rely on assumptions of roughly normal log-returns and relatively stable volatility regimes. In practice, equity returns exhibit fat tails and volatility clustering, meaning actual outcomes fall outside stated intervals more frequently than a naive normal model would suggest. Extended periods of market stress or euphoria can persist long enough to render even month-horizon forecasts quite inaccurate, and my stated intervals should be interpreted as a reasonable central tendency rather than a precise probabilistic guarantee.
